posts.title: Liability Management Ate Operational Restructuring
posts.excerpt: The balance sheet gets fixed in six weeks and the business gets fixed never. That trade is why the same names keep coming back.
posts.plain: There used to be a sequence. posts.body:
There used to be a sequence. A company ran out of room, someone did the work of
figuring out why, and the capital structure got rebuilt around whatever the
business could actually support. The financial fix was downstream of the
operating diagnosis.

That sequence is mostly gone. The financial fix now happens first, fast, and
often instead.

## The numbers say the exchange is the default

Moody's put roughly **65% of private credit defaults in 2025** in the distressed
restructuring bucket. Not chapter 11 — exchanges. The measured default rate for
private credit last year sits anywhere between **1.6% and 4.7%** depending only
on whether you count those exchanges as defaults at all.

That range is the whole story in one statistic. The dominant resolution
mechanism in credit is now a transaction that reasonable people disagree about
whether to call a default.

## What an LME actually buys

Maturity runway and a lower cash coupon. That's it. Both real, both valuable,
neither one an answer to why the business stopped generating cash.

An operational restructuring is slow and unpleasant: you close locations, you
exit product lines, you fight with management about a cost base they built. It
takes quarters and it makes enemies. An uptier takes six weeks, needs a
majority rather than consensus, and pays fees to the people who execute it.

Given those two options and a sponsor whose equity is out of the money, the
choice makes itself. Nobody in the room is incentivized to run the slow one.

## The bill arrives as recidivism

Moody's counted **repeat offenders as roughly 40% of US corporate defaults in
2023**. That number is the price of treating a leverage problem as a maturity
problem.

The mechanism isn't complicated:

1. Company can't service debt because the business is impaired.
2. LME cuts cash interest and pushes maturities out two or three years.
3. Nothing changes operationally, because nothing in the deal required it.
4. Two or three years later, less liquidity, worse docs, fewer assets left
   unencumbered, and a lender group that has already been through one fight.

Round two is always worse than round one. The easy collateral has been pledged,
the unrestricted subsidiary capacity has been used, and the cooperative lenders
have already been sorted from the excluded ones.

## What I'd actually watch

Not the LME announcement. The twelve months after it.

If the exchange comes with a genuine operating plan — new management, closed
footprint, a cost program with dates attached — treat it as a bridge. If it
comes with a press release about "enhanced financial flexibility" and no change
to how the company is run, price it as a delay and start diligencing the next
capital structure now.

The second one is more common, and the market keeps paying full price for it.

---

*Sources: Moody's, [US corporate default risk in 2026](https://www.moodys.com/web/en/us/insights/credit-risk/private-credit/us-corporate-default-risk-in-2026.html); Moody's via [Business Standard](https://www.business-standard.com/amp/world-news/repeat-offenders-made-up-40-of-us-corporate-defaults-in-2023-moody-s-124041601273_1.html) on repeat defaulters.*

posts.title: The 2027 Wall Isn't Big. It's Badly Sorted.
posts.excerpt: Over $700bn of high yield comes due 2027–2029. The size is manageable. What isn't manageable is who's left standing in front of it.
posts.plain: Every maturity wall gets described the same way — a wall — and the framing does the analysis no favors. A wall implies the problem is height. The problem is almost never height. The size, first More than $700 billion of US high yield matures across 2027–2029 , with over $350 billion of that landing in 2029 alone. Add leveraged loans and speculative grade maturities in 2028 alone run to roughly $1 trillion . Big numbers. But 2025 high yield issuance was north of $325 billion , up 17% and the strongest year since 2021. On volume alone, the market clears this. Three years of ordinary issuance covers three years of maturities. If refinancing were purely a capacity question, there would be nothing to discuss. The composition is the whole problem Two facts from 2025 issuance sit uncomfortably together: Over 70% of it was refinancing — the highest share since 2009. Straight CCC paper was under 2% of issuance , the second lowest share on record. Read those in sequence. What remains in front of 2027 and 2028 is the residual — the credits that couldn't clear a market that was wide open and doing record refi volume. The distribution has been sorted, deliberately, by an open market. The issuers approaching 2027 unrefinanced are disproportionately the ones who tried and couldn't, or who looked at the clearing spread and decided to wait. Neither group's situation improves by waiting. What actually breaks first Not the 2027 maturities. The springing covenants and cash sweeps that trigger 12 to 18 months ahead of them, and the auditor conversations about going concern that start roughly the same time. Which means the activity shows up in late 2026 and through 2027 , not on the maturity dates themselves. Distressed situations are created by the approach to a wall, not the collision with it. By the time a bond actually matures, the outcome was decided a year earlier in a room with a lender group. The practical read Stop tracking wall totals. Track: 1. Ratings distribution of what's still outstanding by maturity year. 2. Refi attempts pulled — the deals that launched and didn't price. 3. Extension activity , which is the tell that a full refi wasn't available. The aggregate number tells you the market's capacity. Only the composition tells you who's going to need something other than a refinancing. Sources: PitchBook, 2026 US High Yield Outlook; Octus, 2026 Distressed Outlook.
posts.body:
Every maturity wall gets described the same way — a wall — and the framing does
the analysis no favors. A wall implies the problem is height. The problem is
almost never height.

## The size, first

More than **$700 billion** of US high yield matures across **2027–2029**, with
over **$350 billion** of that landing in 2029 alone. Add leveraged loans and
speculative-grade maturities in 2028 alone run to roughly **$1 trillion**.

Big numbers. But 2025 high yield issuance was **north of $325 billion**, up 17%
and the strongest year since 2021. On volume alone, the market clears this.
Three years of ordinary issuance covers three years of maturities. If refinancing
were purely a capacity question, there would be nothing to discuss.

## The composition is the whole problem

Two facts from 2025 issuance sit uncomfortably together:

- **Over 70% of it was refinancing** — the highest share since 2009.
- **Straight CCC paper was under 2% of issuance**, the second-lowest share on
  record.

Read those in sequence. The market spent 2025 doing almost nothing but
refinancing, and it refinanced almost nothing rated CCC.

Everything that could term out did term out. What remains in front of 2027 and
2028 is the residual — the credits that couldn't clear a market that was wide
open and doing record refi volume.

## Why that matters more than the total

A maturity wall made of BB paper is a scheduling exercise. A maturity wall made
of what's left after three years of adverse selection is a default pipeline.

The distribution has been sorted, deliberately, by an open market. The issuers
approaching 2027 unrefinanced are disproportionately the ones who tried and
couldn't, or who looked at the clearing spread and decided to wait. Neither
group's situation improves by waiting.

## What actually breaks first

Not the 2027 maturities. The **springing covenants and cash sweeps** that trigger
12 to 18 months ahead of them, and the auditor conversations about going concern
that start roughly the same time.

Which means the activity shows up in **late 2026 and through 2027**, not on the
maturity dates themselves. Distressed situations are created by the approach to a
wall, not the collision with it. By the time a bond actually matures, the
outcome was decided a year earlier in a room with a lender group.

## The practical read

Stop tracking wall totals. Track:

1. **Ratings distribution** of what's still outstanding by maturity year.
2. **Refi attempts pulled** — the deals that launched and didn't price.
3. **Extension activity**, which is the tell that a full refi wasn't available.

The aggregate number tells you the market's capacity. Only the composition tells
you who's going to need something other than a refinancing.

---

*Sources: [PitchBook, 2026 US High-Yield Outlook](https://pitchbook.com/news/articles/2026-us-high-yield-outlook-volume-to-tick-higher-amid-looming-maturity-wall); [Octus, 2026 Distressed Outlook](https://octus.com/resources/articles/2026-distressed-outlook/).*

posts.title: Serta Gets a Number: $261m, Plus Six Years of Interest
posts.excerpt: Judge Lopez put a price on an improper uptier. The damages math is more instructive than the liability finding, and it lands almost entirely on prejudgment interest.
posts.plain: On July 7, 2026 , Judge Christopher Lopez in the Southern District of Texas entered judgment against the participating lenders in Serta. The headline number is roughly $400 million . The judgment itself is $261.13 million , and the rest is New York statutory prejudgment interest running at 9% since June 22, 2020 . Sit with that split for a second. Nearly a third of the exposure is the clock. The liability half is now settled law in the Fifth Circuit The 2020 exchange was not an "open market purchase." The court treated it as a payment in respect of principal, which triggered the pro rata sharing provision, which the participating lenders did not satisfy. This is the reading the excluded lenders have been pressing since 2020, and it has now survived all the way through to a damages award. The defense that an open market purchase exception can carry a negotiated, non ratable exchange among a hand picked majority is finished — at least in this circuit. The damages half is where the lesson is The court rejected the models built off Serta's 2023 chapter 11 emergence and valued the breach as of the breach date, marking the first lien loans at 25 cents . That choice does two things: It caps the claim at what the position was worth in June 2020, rather than letting excluded lenders capture the full downstream consequences of the transaction. It front loads the clock , because a 2020 breach date means six years of 9% statutory interest before anyone gets paid. The second effect swamps the first. New York prejudgment interest is not discretionary and it is not compounded at some market rate — it is 9% simple, mandatory, and it accrues whether or not the litigation moves quickly. In a dispute that took six years, that turns a $261m judgment into a $400m one. Two structural details worth noting No joint liability. Each defendant is on the hook for its proportional share of first lien holdings as of June 22, 2020. A participating lender's exposure is a function of its own ticket, not the group's. That materially changes the settlement dynamics — there's no single deep pocket to chase, and no contribution fight among defendants. Breach date valuation cuts both ways. Excluded lenders who assumed damages would be measured against a reorganized enterprise got substantially less than they modeled. Anyone underwriting uptier litigation as a recovery strategy should be running breach date marks, not emergence date ones. Where it goes Expect the Fifth Circuit again. But the practical effect is already priced into how deals get done: the open market purchase exception is now a drafted, fought over provision rather than boilerplate, and the cost of getting it wrong has a public number attached to it for the first time. That number is the useful part. Not the precedent — the invoice. Sources: Vinson & Elkins on the Serta damages judgment; Octus on the damages math and the rejected mitigation defense.
posts.body:
On **July 7, 2026**, Judge Christopher Lopez in the Southern District of Texas
entered judgment against the participating lenders in Serta. The headline number
is roughly **$400 million**. The judgment itself is **$261.13 million**, and the
rest is New York statutory prejudgment interest running at **9% since June 22,
2020**.

Sit with that split for a second. Nearly a third of the exposure is the clock.

## The liability half is now settled law in the Fifth Circuit

The 2020 exchange was not an "open market purchase." The court treated it as a
payment in respect of principal, which triggered the pro rata sharing provision,
which the participating lenders did not satisfy.

This is the reading the excluded lenders have been pressing since 2020, and it
has now survived all the way through to a damages award. The defense that an
open-market-purchase exception can carry a negotiated, non-ratable exchange
among a hand-picked majority is finished — at least in this circuit.

## The damages half is where the lesson is

The court rejected the models built off Serta's 2023 chapter 11 emergence and
valued the breach as of the breach date, marking the first lien loans at **25
cents**.

That choice does two things:

- It **caps the claim** at what the position was worth in June 2020, rather than
  letting excluded lenders capture the full downstream consequences of the
  transaction.
- It **front-loads the clock**, because a 2020 breach date means six years of 9%
  statutory interest before anyone gets paid.

The second effect swamps the first. New York prejudgment interest is not
discretionary and it is not compounded at some market rate — it is 9% simple,
mandatory, and it accrues whether or not the litigation moves quickly. In a
dispute that took six years, that turns a $261m judgment into a $400m one.

## Two structural details worth noting

**No joint liability.** Each defendant is on the hook for its proportional share
of first lien holdings as of June 22, 2020. A participating lender's exposure is
a function of its own ticket, not the group's. That materially changes the
settlement dynamics — there's no single deep pocket to chase, and no
contribution fight among defendants.

**Breach-date valuation cuts both ways.** Excluded lenders who assumed damages
would be measured against a reorganized enterprise got substantially less than
they modeled. Anyone underwriting uptier litigation as a recovery strategy should
be running breach-date marks, not emergence-date ones.

## Where it goes

Expect the Fifth Circuit again. But the practical effect is already priced into
how deals get done: the open-market-purchase exception is now a drafted, fought-over
provision rather than boilerplate, and the cost of getting it wrong has a public
number attached to it for the first time.

That number is the useful part. Not the precedent — the invoice.

---

*Sources: [Vinson & Elkins on the Serta damages judgment](https://www.velaw.com/insights/serta-bankruptcy-court-awards-approximately-400-million-judgment-following-fifth-circuit-uptier-ruling/); [Octus on the damages math and the rejected mitigation defense](https://octus.com/resources/articles/expert-views-the-cost-of-an-improper-uptier-inside-sertas-damages/).*

posts.title: Why This Exists
posts.excerpt: A running notebook on restructuring — dockets, docs, and the arguments that keep repeating.
posts.plain: This is a notebook, not a newsletter. I read a lot of dockets and credit agreements and I want somewhere to put the patterns down before I forget them. Expect posts on chapter 11 mechanics, liability management, creditor coalitions, and the occasional rant about disclosure statements. Nothing here is investment or legal advice.
posts.body:
